candidate.answerReason: The two journey times are 18 and 12 minutes, so the scheduled journey takes 15 minutes. The distance is 12 miles, requiring 48 miles per hour.

methods.label: Compare the travel-time ratios
methods.explanation:
For the same distance, travel time is inversely proportional to speed. Since the speeds \(40\) and \(60\) have ratio \(2:3\), the corresponding travel times have ratio \(3:2\).

The two arrival times differ by six minutes, so the difference of one ratio part is six minutes. The journey therefore takes \(18\) minutes at \(40\) mph and \(12\) minutes at \(60\) mph. Arriving on time requires the midpoint of these durations, namely \(15\) minutes.

The distance to work is
\[
40\left(\frac{18}{60}\right)=12\text{ miles}.
\]
To travel this distance in \(15\) minutes, the required average speed is
\[
\frac{12}{15/60}=48\text{ miles per hour}.
\]
The answer is \(\boxed{48}\), choice B.
methods.levelReason: Inverse proportions, ratios, and time-unit conversions are elementary and within AMC 10 scope.

methods.label: Average the times per mile
methods.explanation:
Because the two arrivals are equally early and late, the desired journey time is the arithmetic mean of the two known journey times. Both journeys cover the same distance, so their average time per mile is also the desired time per mile.

At \(40\) mph, each mile takes \(60/40=1.5\) minutes. At \(60\) mph, each mile takes one minute. The desired time per mile is therefore
\[
\frac{1.5+1}{2}=1.25\text{ minutes}.
\]
At this pace, the number of miles traveled in one hour is
\[
\frac{60}{1.25}=48.
\]
Thus the required average speed is \(\boxed{48}\) miles per hour, choice B.
methods.levelReason: This method uses an arithmetic mean and elementary unit rates, without requiring an additional algebraic formula.

candidate.annotationRationale: The route-neutral relationship is inverse proportionality between speed and duration over a fixed distance. Distance-speed-time relationships and time conversions support both methods. The first route uses proportions to recover the journey durations; the second averages times per mile and avoids finding the distance. The meeting-and-catching-up node is not assigned because those situations do not occur here.

review.mathematicalCheck: The inverse time ratio is 3:2, and the six-minute difference gives durations of 18 and 12 minutes. The scheduled duration is 15 minutes over 12 miles, giving 48 mph. Independently, averaging 1.5 and 1 minute per mile gives 1.25 minutes per mile, also 48 mph.
review.levelCheck: Both methods use elementary ratios, arithmetic means, and unit conversions. The midpoint reasoning is explained.
